newsitem.title: UK: British business despairs of govt Euro bickering.
newsitem.headline: British business despairs of govt Euro bickering.

text.p: British business leaders have thrown their hands up in horror at the latest spat of government in-fighting over Europe.
Whether Britain signs up for a single European currency or not, the business community is desperate for a rational debate, not one that alienates the public and Britain's European partners alike.

"These sorts of comments don't help the UK's credibility in negotiations on the single currency," said Ian Peters, deputy director-general of the British Chambers of Commerce. "Neither does it help foster a wider debate in the business community."

He was talking about another eruption of government infighting, triggered on Wednesday by Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind who said that on balance the government was hostile to European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, the most pro-European member of the government, dismissed the comments as a "slip of the tongue".
And Prime Minister John Major was dragged into the argument, stressing that the government's wait-and-see policy over European economic and monetary union remained in place.
Later that night, Clarke and Rifkind issued a joint statement to Reuters agreeing that there was no change to the government's policy. But by then the damage had been done.

"If the government is saying it is hostile to EMU, we really don't think that's helpful," Peters said. "Business is confused about where the government actually stands and if we are, heaven knows what our European partners think."
The British Chambers of Commerce, which represents some 200,000 companies from all sectors, thinks it is vital for the British government to retain a voice at the heart of Europe.

Peters said the government was right to keep its options open over a single currency, scheduled to start on January 1, 1999 but it must stay at the negotiation table either way, to avoid isolation. "It's important that we have the credibility to negotiate effectively. There is a danger of that being compromised," he said.

The Confederation of British Industry, Britain's top employers' organisation, takes a similar line. Writing in the Daily Express on Monday, before the Rifkind-Clarke row blew up, CBI director-general Adair Turner said Britain needed a "full and constructive" membership of the EU, arguing from within for the changes it wanted to see.
The CBI also backs a wait-and-see policy over EMU, but is in no doubt that Europhobic rhetoric is extremely damaging.
Turner said Britain could opt out of the first wave of EMU and stay at the heart of Europe as long as it adopted a positive attitude and kept the option open of joining later.
"But if we stay out amid triumphalist assertions of our superiority and against the background of a wider Europhobia, we risk isolation," he said.

Britain's membership of the European single market has helped to attract inward investment from around the globe, "which since 1980 has created 700,000 jobs directly and millions more indirectly," he said.
The chiefs of Japanese car giant Toyota and food-to-detergents group Unilever recently warned that they may rethink their investments in Britain if it ducked out of EMU.
Ruth Lea, head of the Institute of Directors' Policy Unit, said those sort of companies, big on inward investment, were likely to be pro-EMU and the cheaper trade costs it offers.

"Small businesses, dependent on the British economy, are much more likely to be anti. It matters to them more that the economy remains in good shape." She said 70 percent of IoD members were anti-EMU.

But they may take comfort from the government's European wrangles. "We feel that in the government, with the exception of Clarke and (deputy prime minister Michael) Heseltine, there is really very little commitment to early entry," Lea said.
